title: Dual-path propagation shim and sampling reconciliation
creator: Aisha Raman
body: Summary: Implement a dual-path propagation shim in our language SDKs and middleware that simultaneously maintains compatibility with legacy header carriers and a compact, binary-safe envelope for high-throughput internal paths (websockets, worker-queues). The shim must reconcile sampling decisions across hops and produce consistent span IDs when requests traverse mixed clients (legacy HTTP, new SDKs, third-party proxies). The feature reduces gap-caused orphaned spans, improves tail-latency visibility for short-lived internal RPCs, and avoids double-sampling explosions in high-traffic routes.
background: We observe incorrect trace stitching and spikes in sampled span counts for services behind legacy proxies and for multi-hop websocket flows. Root causes: header name fragmentation, divergent sampling decisions at each hop, and loss of sampling metadata in binary frames. Current SDKs attempt best-effort header copying but lack a deterministic reconciliation policy. This ticket centralizes a deterministic, low-overhead reconciliation logic in SDKs and server middleware so traces remain coherent without adding significant per-request CPU or header bloat.
acceptance_criteria: 1) SDKs (Go, Python, Node) implement the shim and pass compatibility tests with legacy header carriers (traceparent, b3, x-request-id) and new compact envelope. 2) Multi-hop websocket and queue-based integration tests show span continuity across hops. 3) Sampling rate metrics for critical routes show no >5% increase in sampled tokens after rollout. 4) No latency regression >2ms P95 on instrumented middleware. 5) Feature gated and gradually rolled out per-service with telemetry to verify correctness.
design_notes:
- Carrier format: keep existing textual header names for external compatibility; add a single base64-encoded X-RW-TRACE envelope for internal frames with fields: trace_id, parent_id, flags, sampling_hash, and a version byte. Envelope size target < 80 bytes.
- Reconciliation policy: deterministic sampling precedence: 1) explicit deny flag, 2) explicit force-sample flag, 3) highest sampling_priority from carriers, 4) local sampler tied to sampling_hash (consistent hashing on trace_id + service_id) when undecided.
- ID canonicalization: derive canonical parent_id using xor-mix of incoming parent_id and local ephemeral id when parent_id absent to avoid duplicate root spans.
- Performance: parsing envelope on a hot path must use a fast path that avoids allocation for well-formed frames; fallback to safe parsing when validation fails.
- Backcompat: if both legacy headers and envelope present, envelope takes precedence but we populate legacy headers on outbound HTTP calls for downstream compatibility.
- Metrics: emit reconciliation.counter with labels {outcome:reconciled|conflict|invalid, carrier:legacy|envelope|mixed}, and sampling.decisions by service and route.
tradeoffs_and_alternatives:
1) Option A: Server-side-only reconciliation (simpler rollout) — rejected because it leaves many clients producing incompatible carriers.
2) Option B: Global header normalization at edge proxies — high coordination cost and risk to customer-owned proxies.
3) Option C: Full binary protocol change — too disruptive.
Chosen: implement shim in SDKs + middleware with opt-in feature flag for Private/Dedicated customers initially.
implementation_steps: Spec review and approval by Security and Observability teams
Prototype shim in Go SDK and middleware with unit tests
Add same shim to Node and Python SDKs (prioritized order: Go -> Node -> Python)
Integration tests for websocket and queue paths
Performance microbenchmarks and P95 latency guardrails
Documentation for SDK changelog + migration guide
Canary rollout to two low-risk services, collect reconciliation metrics
Gradual rollout with toggled feature flags and automated rollback conditions
rollout_plan: Phase 1: feature-gated build available to internal services and Dedicated customers (2 weeks). Phase 2: canary on infra services (2 weeks) with automated checks (sampling.rate delta, reconciliation.conflicts < 0.5%). Phase 3: broad SDK release with opt-out via env var for customers (4 weeks). Post-rollout: default on in next minor runtime release (runtime-1.22).
testing_plan:
- Unit tests: carrier parsing, precedence, sampling_hash computation, invalid envelope handling.
- Integration tests: end-to-end trace continuity across HTTP->websocket->worker queue.
- Load tests: verify CPU and allocation impact under 10k rps, assert P95 latency < baseline +2ms.
- Fuzzer: random envelope corruption to confirm graceful degradation and metric emission.
- Security tests: ensure envelope cannot be used to escalate privileges or leak secrets; validate signature/nonce plan in future iteration.
monitoring_and_metrics: Key metrics: tracing.reconciliation.count, tracing.reconciliation.conflicts, tracing.sampling.rate_per_route, tracing.orphan_span_rate_per_service, middleware.latency_ms_p95. Dashboards: new 'Propagation Reconciliation' dashboard (per-cluster and per-route) and alert: reconciliation.conflicts > 1% sustained for 10m -> send SLO and platform team pager.
open_questions: Do we sign the envelope for intra-cluster trust (tradeoff: CPU + key rotation complexity)?
Should the envelope version include an origin service id to assist replay protection?
How aggressively should we backpopulate legacy headers on outbound high-cardinality routes (cost vs compatibility)?
security_considerations: Envelope contains only trace identifiers and sampling flags. No PII. Security review required to validate that an attacker cannot manipulate sampling to bypass audit trails or cause volume amplification. Possible mitigations: per-cluster HMAC in later phase, rate-limiting reconciliation conflicts to avoid overloaded metrics pipelines.
